links.note: Pre-reading choice between dense forests, magical lands, busy cities or quiet places - the self-survey that leads into why people take up adventure, not a detail of the tunnel story.
Pre-reading choice between climbing a mountain, hunting treasure, solving puzzles or building a model - the same adventure-preference survey, so 28308.
Pre-reading item on teamwork, resolving into Bold Explorer / Imaginative Dreamer / Energetic Planner - what disposes people to adventure.
The watchman's name - Sunder Singh. Identifies the man whose encounter with the leopard is 28298.
The time of day at the start - almost noon, when Suraj waits at the cutting for the midday train. Part of the frame in 28297.
Listening announcement about the Adventure Club trip, its in-charge and its three-day length - exactly the trip-planning material 28307 describes.
Letter to the Principal requesting an excursion to a hill station, giving the reason and the arrangements - the trip-planning task of 28307.
How the speaker's imagination brings trains to life in the first two stanzas - the pull of journeys the poem sets out.
Where the railroad track is - miles away, and yet the speaker hears the train. The poem's longing, not a story detail.
What is common to the busy day and the still night - the train's presence in the speaker's mind, which is the poem's wish to travel.
How the speaker feels about her friends - warm affection, set against her urge to leave. Part of the poem's argument about travelling.
What the speaker sees in imagination at night - red cinders against the sky. The poem's imagined journeys.
What the speaker hears by day despite the noisy voices - the whistle shrieking. The poem's pull towards travel.
Identify sound imagery in the poem - 'its whistle shrieking', 'its engine steaming'. A question about what was heard as selected detail, which is 28304.
Which stanza focuses on the speaker's friendships - the third. The poem's structure of longing against attachment.
The contradiction in the speaker's feelings - she wants to leave although she loves her friends. The poem's wish to travel.
How far the railroad track is from the poet - miles away, yet she attends to every train. The poem's longing.
What is loud with voices speaking during the day - the setting against which the speaker still hears the train.
What the poet sees red on the sky at night - its cinders. The poem's imagined train.
What the poet hears the engine doing at night - steaming. The poem's imagined train.
With whom the poet's heart is warm - the friends she makes, the tie the wish to travel pulls against.
What kind of friends she says she'll not be knowing - better ones. The counterweight to the poem's travel longing.
What beats out a steady rhythm on the rails at night - the carriage wheels. A detail of the journey the speaker wants.
The poet's sentiment about friendships - warmth and contentment, held against the urge to board any train.
What time of day the second stanza describes - night. The poem's structure of day and night longing.
What the night is usually associated with in the poem - dreams and sleep, which the train keeps interrupting.
What the speaker imagines at night despite no train passing - cinders and steam. The poem's persistent wish to travel.
What the speaker's heart is filled with - friends. The attachment the poem weighs against leaving.
What is ironic in her attitude to her friends - she values them yet still wants to leave. The poem's central tension.
The device in 'I see its cinders red on the sky' - imagery. A question about a selected visual detail, so 28304 rather than 28305's theme.
The main theme - longing for travel and new experiences. 28305 states precisely that.
The moral of the poem and how the speaker's attitude reflects it - curiosity and openness alongside friendship.
The role of train imagery - whistles, sparks, steam - in conveying the adventurous spirit. About sensory detail doing the work of description.
Assertion-reason on 'My heart is warm with the friends I make' and whether it is about staying home. The poem's travel longing against attachment.
What Arunima did to pursue Everest - the mountaineering course at Uttarkashi, eighteen months of training, Bachendri Pal's guidance. The road from the accident to the peak.
Listening task matching speakers' opinions on adventure sports, including one who finds exposure to risks unnecessary - exactly 28308's discussion of why people undertake adventure.
Synonym for 'summit' - peak. A glossary item from the Arunima text, the same vocabulary strand as beacon and resilience.
Who instilled confidence in Arunima - Bachendri Pal, her guide in the climb. Part of the journey to the highest peak.
Her mother's occupation, health supervisor - background to the twenty-four-year-old whose life the 2011 event altered.
Arunima's passion for sports - the national-level volleyball player of 28309, before the accident.
